title: CoreWeave: the backlog is real; the equity is a levered bet on refinancing it
subtitle: Initiation. Revenue is compounding at more than 110% a year against a US$104bn backlog, but most of the build-out is funded with borrowed money that the bond market now prices near distress. Our four scenarios run from a restructuring (about US$0) to about US$258 a share. Weighted, they give about US$69, 13% above the US$61.39 close, with a 55% chance of losing three-quarters of the equity or more. We start at Neutral, with Very high risk.
author: GIVA Research (AI-assisted)

stance.label: Neutral
stance.horizon: About 14 months, to end-2027 (our valuation date). Checkpoints: Q3 FY2026 results (around 9–10 Nov 2026) and FY2026 results with the FY2027 capex guide (around late Feb 2027)
stance.summary: The fundamentals are not the problem: Q2 FY2026 revenue rose **112% y/y** to US$2.58bn and RPO reached **US$103.7bn** [s2,s8]. The funding is: net debt of about **US$29.8bn** on **US$5.0bn** of equity [s8,s57], interest of US$640m a quarter heading to about US$900m [s9], and unsecured bonds yielding about 15% [s28,s31]. Our probability-weighted value is about **US$69** a share against the US$61.39 close [s25], but 55% of the weight sits in a restructuring or a funding-constrained bear case that leaves the equity worth US$4 or less. Whether CoreWeave can fund its 2027 plan on acceptable terms will largely be settled inside our horizon, and we have no edge over the credit market on that, so we start at Neutral.

highlights: **Fundamental growth is not the debate.** Revenue rose from US$229m in FY2023 to US$5.13bn in FY2025 and US$7.59bn TTM; Q2 FY2026 grew 112% y/y, and FY2026 guidance was raised to US$12.4–13.2bn [s1,s2,s9].

**Financing is the debate.** TTM operating cash flow of US$6.9bn covered about a third of US$20.6bn of cash capex, and the company plans US$35–39bn of capex in 2026 on its own definition [s2,s9]. Interest expense rose from US$267m (Q2 FY2025) to US$640m (Q2 FY2026), with US$860–940m guided for Q3 [s8,s9].

**The October slide started in the credit market, but it is not only sentiment.** Shares fell about 25% in the week to 16 Oct as unsecured yields reached about 15% and five-year CDS hit a record of about 1,195bp intraday [s27,s28,s34]. For a company that can only grow by borrowing, the cost of funding is a fundamental input, and two demand datapoints turned too: OpenAI’s lower net revenue run-rate and Reuters’ report of hyperscaler capex-delay signals [s35,s47]. Reported results did not miss.

**Valuation is a levered residual with a real tail.** Our base case (FY2028 adj. EBITDA US$23.6bn at 7x, net debt about US$78bn by end-2027) is worth about US$119 a share; a funding-constrained bear case about US$4; a restructuring about nothing. Weighted 15/40/35/10 with the bull case (about US$258), that is about US$69. Each turn of EV/EBITDA moves the base case by about US$32 a share.

**Revenue concentration is falling; backlog concentration is not.** The largest customer fell from 71% to 36% of revenue in a year, but on disclosed contract ceilings Meta (about US$35bn) and OpenAI (about US$22bn) are roughly a third and a fifth of the US$103.7bn RPO. OpenAI-backed capacity is financed in a non-investment-grade facility that cannot use the A3-rated DDTL 4.0 template [s2,s17,s19,s103,s110].

blocks.text: CoreWeave rents NVIDIA GPU capacity, mostly on multi-year take-or-pay contracts, to AI labs and hyperscalers [s1,s84]. Revenue was **US$5.13bn in FY2025 (+168%)** and **US$2.58bn in Q2 FY2026 alone (+112% y/y)** [s1,s2]. Contracted demand is visible: RPO was **US$103.7bn** at 30 June 2026, and management reported more than US$25bn of further commitments signed early in Q3 [s2,s8].

The equity case turns on the other side of the balance sheet. Most of the build-out is financed with debt raised against GPUs and customer contracts: operating cash flow covered about a third of cash capex over the last twelve months, and NVIDIA added US$2bn of equity in January [s2,s62]. Debt was about **US$35.1bn** at 30 June 2026 against **US$5.0bn** of equity [s2,s57]. Interest already exceeds adjusted operating income: US$640m against US$128m in Q2 [s8], with Q3 guidance of US$860–940m against US$200–260m [s9]. S&P rates the issuer B+, with a positive outlook [s117]. The company is exposed less to demand than to the price and availability of credit, and in October that price moved sharply against it [s28,s31].

blocks.text: **Why Neutral.** Our weighted value is about 13% above the share price, but the distribution is close to binary: 55% of the weight sits in a restructuring or in a funding-constrained bear case worth about US$4, and 45% in cases worth about US$119–258. Which side CoreWeave lands on turns on funding roughly US$50bn of cash needs through end-2027 (Section 8), and the answer will largely be known inside our horizon, once the FY2027 capex and funding plan is out. We have no edge over the credit market on that outcome, and small changes in our weights move the weighted value by about as much as the gap to the price: each 5 points moved from the bear to the base case adds about US$6. To stress-test these assumptions, including the interest-rate path, use the interactive model in Section 9. Its outcome distribution weights each business risk and upside by its own probability, links them through a boom, normal or bust regime (so a funding squeeze and an AI capex air pocket tend to come together) and draws the exit multiple, cost of equity, unit costs, sell-through and GPU life as well: it centres at about US$76 a share (P10 about US$17, P90 about US$142), with about 38% of outcomes below the share price, close to this weighting. **Why not Cautious.** Reported results have not missed: Q2 beat consensus revenue, guidance went up and the backlog grew [s8,s24]. A successful investment-grade financing of the 2027 plan would cut the cost of capital sharply (DDTL 4.0 priced at SOFR + 225bp [s17]).

blocks.title: What would make us more positive
blocks.text: Q3 FY2026 revenue at or above the US$3.45–3.60bn guide with interest inside US$860–940m [s9]; an FY2027 capex plan funded mainly through investment-grade, contract-backed facilities like DDTL 4.0 rather than unsecured paper near 15% [s17,s28]; an upgrade from S&P’s B+ toward the investment-grade profile management says it is targeting [s109,s117]; and a sustained fall in CDS from the October record [s31].

blocks.title: What would make us Cautious
blocks.text: Refinancing at unsecured yields near current levels; any cash-trap event under a GPU facility [s61]; another capex raise without matching revenue; re-scoping of an OpenAI or Microsoft contract [s35]; another data-centre delivery delay like November 2025’s [s114]; or equity issuance well beyond the 35m-share at-the-market programme [s109].

**Model.** CoreWeave sells GPU compute by the hour or, mostly, under committed multi-year contracts. Average contract length rose from about four to about five years during 2025 [s84]. Customers prepay part of the contract value, which is why deferred revenue reached US$9.7bn at 30 June 2026 [s2]. Each large contract is typically financed in its own special-purpose vehicle with a delayed-draw term loan (DDTL) secured on the GPUs and the contract cash flows, which pay operating costs and lenders before the parent [s17,s103]. One secondary source describes a cash trap in DDTL 3.0 if a key customer seriously breaches its contract [s61]; we have not checked that against the credit agreement. In Q3 FY2026 the company began signing short-dated (3–6 month) capacity at about US$40m of annualised revenue per MW, which it described as higher pricing [s16,s37]. For scale, Q2 revenue ran at about US$7m a year per active MW (US$2.58bn × 4 ÷ about 1.5 GW, our arithmetic [s2,s10]); most existing capacity is locked in at fixed contract prices, so the uplift reaches revenue slowly.

**Platform.** Beyond bare-metal GPUs, the stack includes CoreWeave Kubernetes Service, Slurm-on-Kubernetes (SUNK), Mission Control for fleet operations, and developer tools from acquisitions: Weights & Biases (completed May 2025) [s22], OpenPipe and Marimo [s102]. A planned all-stock takeover of Core Scientific was voted down by that company’s shareholders on 30 October 2025 [s23]. CoreWeave still leases about 590 MW from Core Scientific across six sites under 12-year hosting contracts [s115], which makes it the company’s largest landlord.

blocks.caption: Footprint and power
blocks.note: Active power was about 41% of contracted power at 30 June 2026 (our arithmetic): most of the contracted capacity still has to be built, energised and financed. Capacity is mostly leased colocation; the first self-built site is due in 2026 [s81].

blocks.text: **Revenue drivers.** Revenue is power times price times billing. About 98% comes from take-or-pay contracts of about five years, so revenue risk sits at delivery and at renewal rather than in whether customers use what they signed for [s3,s143]. What moves it: (1) how many megawatts go live, and when: about 1.5 GW was active at 30 June against 4.2 GW contracted by August [s10], and a late building moves revenue right, as in November 2025 [s145]; (2) the price per megawatt: about US$10.4m per billing MW-year in Q2 2026 (our arithmetic [s2]), with short-dated deals near US$40m [s16]; newer GPUs earn more per hour but fit fewer per megawatt, so the long-term rate is steady; (3) billing: a new site pays rent and power for one to two months before it bills [s143]; and (4) renewals, which touch only a small part of the fleet each year before 2031 (“a very limited part of our fleet” [s10]; 1–6% a year in our model). Costs scale with the same megawatts: about US$3m of cost of revenue per active MW-year (rent was 59% and power 21% of the FY2025 increase) and about US$35–36m of capex per MW [s1,s2,s142]. CoreWeave rents its buildings and owns what is inside them, the fast-depreciating part [s213]. Section 9 builds the projections from these drivers, with the risks and upsides to each.

**NVIDIA is supplier, shareholder, customer and backstop at once.** It supplies the GPUs, anchored the IPO and invested a further US$2bn at US$87.20 a share in January 2026 [s62,s63]. Under a September 2025 order it must buy any capacity CoreWeave cannot sell, up to US$6.3bn through April 2032 [s20]. On 15 October its CEO said CoreWeave was "improving every day" and needed no backstop [s32]. The arrangement supports demand in a downturn, but it also ties CoreWeave’s fortunes to a single supplier’s strategy.

**Governance.** Class B shares carry ten votes. At 31 July 2026 Class B was about 17% of shares and about 67% of votes, held by the founders [s55]. Founders and early investors have been heavy sellers since the IPO, mostly under 10b5-1 plans [s53,s96].

**Controls and litigation.** The FY2025 10-K reports material weaknesses in internal control over financial reporting (IT general controls, segregation of duties and accounting staffing) that still existed at 31 December 2025, with remediation expected to continue through 2026 [s1]. Every statement figure in this report rests on those filings. A securities class action (Masaitis v. CoreWeave, D.N.J. No. 2:26-cv-00355, class period 28 March to 15 December 2025) alleges the company understated its reliance on a single third-party data-centre supplier; we have not tracked its current status [s116].

**Demand.** The four largest US platforms (Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet, Meta) guided combined 2026 capex of more than US$700bn [s78]; in May Moody’s raised its 2026 hyperscaler forecast to about US$785bn, with 2027 approaching US$1tn [s215]. Neoclouds take the overflow, and Microsoft has been CoreWeave’s largest customer [s56]. Frontier labs (OpenAI, Meta, Anthropic) are the other demand pool [s18,s19,s92].

**Doubts.** In October the sector’s sentiment turned on three things. OpenAI told investors its annualised revenue was about US$50bn, below the widely reported US$68bn, which had counted revenue booked by its partners [s35]. Reuters reported hints of data-centre project delays and slower capex growth from hyperscalers, and that Gartner ranks CoreWeave first of about 100 neoclouds on exposure to the gap between revenue and capital spending [s47]. And Gartner forecast that more than 80% of neocloud providers will be forced to cease independent operations by 2030 [s29,s30].

blocks.text: **Where CoreWeave is strong.** It has the largest backlog, it is usually first to deploy new NVIDIA platforms, and it was first to raise investment-grade financing against GPU contracts (DDTL 4.0, rated A3 by Moody’s and backed by Meta contracts) [s17,s60]. **Where it is weak.** It owns little of its real estate or power, its cost of unsecured capital is high, and two counterparties hold most of its disclosed backlog (Section 6).

**Power and delivery.** Delivery risk is not theoretical. On 10 November 2025 CoreWeave cut FY2025 revenue guidance from US$5.15–5.35bn to US$5.05–5.15bn because a third-party data-centre developer (reported to be Core Scientific) ran late, and the shares fell sharply the next day [s13,s114]; FY2025 revenue landed at US$5.13bn [s1]. With active power at about 41% of contracted power at 30 June 2026 (Section 2), most of the backlog still depends on landlords and utilities delivering on time. Our bear case assumes they deliver late and the company cannot fund the rest at acceptable cost.

**GPU useful life: how much of the EBITDA is real?** CoreWeave depreciates technology equipment over six years [s1]; secondary coverage reports that it lengthened that life from five to six years from 1 January 2023, which we have not confirmed in the filings [s85]. Critics argue the economic life of AI GPUs is closer to two or three years [s85]. Depreciation is the largest cost line: about US$1.4bn in Q2 FY2026, 54% of revenue [s2]. The table rescales Q2 depreciation to shorter lives, holding everything else equal.

blocks.text: A shorter life does not change cash flow, but it changes two things that matter here. First, maintenance: to hold a given EBITDA, the fleet has to be replaced on its economic life, not its book life, so EBITDA overstates owner earnings by the gap. Second, collateral: GPU loans are sized against contracts of about five years and amortise from contract cash flows [s17,s84], so lenders are exposed to what a GPU is worth when its first contract ends. If renewal prices for Hopper-generation fleets reset sharply lower, the residual value that the next financing leans on falls with them. We reflect this in a below-peer 7x base multiple and in the bear case’s lower FY2028 margin (Section 8) rather than in a DCF.

The company reported material weaknesses in internal control over financial reporting at 31 December 2025 (Section 2) [s1], so we use the filings as filed and mark figures that rest on rounded inputs. Two definitional differences matter, and we show both versions: **capex** (XBRL records cash paid; the company’s headline figure also includes accrued and vendor-financed additions) and **EBITDA** (our GAAP proxy versus the company’s adjusted figure).

blocks.text: **Fundamental growth troughed at about 110%, and guidance implies re-acceleration.** Year-on-year revenue growth fell from 420% in Q1 FY2025 to 110% in Q4 FY2025, then held at 112% in each of the first two quarters of 2026. Sequential growth picked up to 32% in Q1 FY2026 and 24% in Q2 [s2,s3]. The Q3 guide midpoint of US$3.53bn implies about 158% y/y and 37% q/q, and the FY2026 midpoint of US$12.8bn about 149% [s9]. The debate is whether the second-half ramp is delivered on time, given the November 2025 delay (Section 3).

blocks.text: **Margins are compressing.** Revenue less cost of revenue (which excludes depreciation) fell from about 73–76% through Q3 FY2025 to 67.6% in Q4 FY2025 and about 66% in the first half of 2026. We have not confirmed management’s explanation; the likeliest driver is lease and power cost on capacity that is energised before it earns full revenue (operating lease cost was about US$500m in Q2 FY2026, against about US$180m a year earlier, per the 10-Q [s2]). Gross-profit growth (88% y/y in Q2 FY2026) is now well below revenue growth (112%). Operating margin was negative in three of the last four quarters, because depreciation arrives as soon as capacity is energised, before the revenue ramps [s2].

blocks.text: **Cash flow and capex intensity.** Over the twelve months to June 2026, operating cash flow was US$6.9bn (91% of revenue, flattered by customer prepayments) and cash capex was US$20.6bn (271% of revenue), for free cash flow of **−US$13.7bn** [s2]. On the company’s capex definition the burn is larger: H1 FY2026 company-defined capex was about US$17.1bn against US$3.7bn of operating cash flow [s2,s8,s83]. The full-year plan of US$35–39bn means roughly US$20bn more to fund in the second half [s9].

blocks.text: Capex guidance for 2026 was raised twice, from US$30–35bn to US$31–35bn in May and to US$35–39bn in August, while revenue guidance rose only at the edges [s9,s83]. Part of that capex is for revenue in 2027 and beyond, but until the ratio turns, every revenue beat brings a larger financing need.

blocks.text: **Interest burden.** Interest expense rose from US$361m in FY2024 to US$1,229m in FY2025 and US$640m in Q2 FY2026 alone, against US$267m a year earlier [s8,s12]. Q3 guidance of US$860–940m is about four times guided adjusted operating income of US$200–260m [s9]. Measured against adjusted EBITDA, interest absorbed 40% in FY2025 and 42% in Q2 FY2026 (our arithmetic from [s8,s12]). Fixed-charge cover is thin: in Q2, adjusted EBITDA plus rent covered interest plus rent about 1.8 times (our arithmetic from [s2,s8]). Because most secured debt floats over SOFR, rates feed straight into the interest line: the Fed raised its target range by 25bp to 3.75–4.00% on 16 September, its first hike since 2023 [s111], and the hot September CPI print raised the odds of another move at the 27–28 October meeting [s87].

**Maturities and liquidity.** US$7.5bn of debt was classified as current at 30 June 2026 [s57], and one secondary source puts principal due by end-2027 at US$10.6bn [s58]. DDTL debt amortises from contract cash flows, so the more relevant refinancing exposure is the unsecured notes and any facility whose cash is trapped. The company did breach covenants on a 2024 loan, which triggered technical defaults that were later waived [s91]. Cash was US$5.5bn at 30 June. The September convertible closed at US$4.2bn with the option exercised: net proceeds were about US$4.14bn, and after about US$0.57bn of capped calls it added about US$3.57bn of cash before offering expenses [s39,s108].

**Dilution.** Class A plus Class B shares were 551.5m at 31 July 2026, up from 545.6m at 30 April [s3,s55]; implied weighted basic shares were 200.7m in FY2024 and 424.4m in FY2025 (IPO and conversions) [s1]. Ahead: the ATM programme (up to 35m shares, about 6% of the count) [s109]; three convertibles, of which the 2033s convert into about 42.9m shares at US$97.85 and the 2032s into roughly 33m at about US$119.60 (the 2031s’ conversion terms we have not confirmed), each with capped calls that offset dilution up to their caps [s14,s105,s106,s107]; and stock-based compensation of US$619m over the last twelve months, 8.2% of revenue [s2]. We treat all three convertibles as debt in every scenario (Section 8).

blocks.title: Credit market, week of 12–16 October
blocks.text: The 9.625% 2032 notes traded below 80 cents for a yield near 15%, and the 2031s yielded about 15.8% on 15 October [s28,s31]. Five-year CDS reached a record of about 1,195bp intraday before settling near 1,040bp [s31,s34]. S&P rates the issuer B+ with a positive outlook [s117]. Equity holders sit below roughly US$35bn of debt at 30 June, more after the September convertible, that the market prices as high yield bordering on distressed. Section 8 sets the equity discount rate separately from these yields.

At Q1 the company said about 36% of backlog would be recognised within 24 months [s95]. On the Q1 call (7 May 2026) management said ten customers had each committed at least US$1bn, and that non-investment-grade AI-native companies and labs were under 30% of backlog [s143].

sections.title: Recent share-price performance: what drove the slide

blocks.text: From a post-earnings close of about US$108 on 12 August (a single source) [s40] the shares fell to **US$61.39 on 16 October** [s25,s26], about **−43%**. Most of the fall came in the week of 12–16 October, when the shares lost about a quarter of their value [s27]. CNBC’s quote page showed a 52-week high of US$150.40, set on 16 October 2025, so that high was rolling out of the window on our data date [s42]. The October slide also retraced a rebound: the shares had fallen about 26% in the five sessions to 29 July [s113] before rallying on the August results. Since August the move had three legs: a five-session fall of about 19% to 15 September, ahead of the Fed’s 16 September hike [s111,s112]; the convertible-plus-ATM financing on 17 September; and an October cascade that started in the credit market.

blocks.text: **Interpretation.** The slide started in the credit market: unsecured yields moved from 9–10% coupons to about 15% and CDS reached a record [s28,s31]. That is not only sentiment. For a company that can only grow by borrowing, the cost and availability of funding are fundamental inputs, and two demand datapoints also turned against it: OpenAI’s lower net run-rate and Reuters’ hyperscaler capex-delay signals [s35,s47]. Reported results did not miss: the last quarter beat on revenue and raised guidance [s8,s24]. The fall was also sector-wide: Nebius, IREN, Oracle and the semiconductor index fell alongside, and CoreWeave, the most levered name, fell most [s25,s48]. Sell-side defenders included Cantor (Overweight, US$176), JPMorgan ("overdone") and Deutsche Bank [s46,s70,s93].

CoreWeave has no earnings to put a P/E on, so we value it on enterprise value against forward adjusted EBITDA, and we treat the equity explicitly as what is left after debt. Spot inputs: **US$61.39** close [s25] × **551.5m** shares [s55] = **US$33.9bn** market cap; plus **US$29.8bn** net debt at 30 June [s57] = **US$63.6bn** spot EV (our arithmetic). We treat all three convertibles as debt, assuming net-share settlement: principal is repaid like debt, and the capped calls offset the conversion spread up to their caps [s14,s106].

blocks.text: **Choosing the multiple.** The asset-light names above are not the right anchor: their EBITDA is not consumed by depreciation and their balance sheets are investment grade. The closer economic comparables are lessors of depreciating, debt-financed equipment on contracts (aircraft lessors, equipment rental), with contracted data-centre landlords as an upper bound for longer-dated contracts on longer-lived assets. We did not find dated, citable multiples for those groups in time for this report, so we show none. Our 7x base multiple is about Oracle’s next-twelve-months multiple (8.6x FY May-2027 and 6.0x FY May-2028 on 18 October, ~7.2x blended [s72]) and well below the asset-light peers; the bear case uses 5.5x, a distressed-credit level.

**Method.** We value the company at end-2027 on a one-year-forward multiple of FY2028 adjusted EBITDA, roll net debt forward with guidance and consensus cash flows, and discount the per-share value back 1.2 years at an **18% cost of equity**. That rate is a stated premium (roughly the 3.75–4.00% policy rate [s111] plus about 14 points for a single-B, pre-profit, highly levered equity), not a read-across from the bond yield: a 15% yield on near-distressed bonds is a promised yield, not an expected return. Default risk sits in the scenario weights, so the high rate is partly a second, conservative haircut; at 15% or 21% the weighted value would be about US$71 or US$67. Step 1 is common to all cases: from US$29.8bn at 30 June, H2 FY2026 company-defined capex of about US$20.9bn (guide midpoint US$37bn less H1 US$16.1bn [s9,s142,s143]), H2 adjusted EBITDA of about US$4.9bn (consensus FY US$7.55bn [s65] less H1 US$2.67bn [s8,s11]), interest of about US$1.9bn and US$1.5bn of prepayments take **net debt to about US$46.2bn by end-2026**. After that, any equity raised is credited against net debt, so new shares are not counted twice. Section 9 builds revenue from capacity instead. On this section’s convention (FY2028 EBITDA, including the MW built during 2028) its base gives about US$124 a share: its capacity-built FY2028 adjusted EBITDA (about US$24.4bn) outweighs paying stock-based compensation in new shares (about 628m shares at end-2027). On its own default it values only the fleet in place at end-2027 (3.1 GW at FY2028 economics, about US$22.3bn of run-rate EBITDA, against the net debt that paid for it), which gives about US$105.

blocks.text: **Does the backlog cover the debt on its own?** We test the "backlog is real" half of the thesis by stopping growth: no capex after the committed 2026 build, revenue held at the roughly US$19bn exit-2026 run-rate [s9] for five years (about the average contract length [s84]), a 59% EBITDA margin [s8], and the US$9.7bn of customer prepayments already received [s2] unwinding over the period. Contracted cash flow pays the interest and cuts net debt from about US$46bn to about US$19bn by end-2031, but it does not clear it. In run-off, the equity is worth roughly the residual value of five-year-old GPUs plus the value of renewing contracts, less about US$19bn of debt, before discounting. The backlog is real; on its own it does not make the equity safe.

blocks.text: This section turns the report’s assumptions into a working model, and revenue in it is no longer a growth rate: it is built from what can be watched each quarter [s213]. **Capacity**: active power reaches 1.87 GW at end-2026 (the guide), then 3.1, 4.2, 5.1 and 6.0 GW, against 3.7 GW of contracted power at 30 June and 4.2 GW at 11 August [s142,s10] and the sites in the model’s capacity table. **Billing**: a megawatt bills about two months after it goes live [s143], and 95–100% of it bills (our path; 2026 is largely sold out [s143]). **Contracts first**: the signed backlog bills first, take-or-pay at its contract price, once its capacity is live; price, utilisation and sell-through stresses act only on capacity not yet under contract (new MW and expiring contracts), and only a delivery slip or a customer cancelling takes contracted revenue below its schedule. **Price**: about US$11m of revenue per billing MW-year (US$10.5m in Q3 and US$11.3m in Q4 2026 land the Q3 guide and the exit-2026 run-rate guide [s9]). **Renewals**: 1–6% of the fleet re-signs each year at 10–20% below its old price (our estimates: renewals are “a very limited part of our fleet”, and Hopper re-contracting has priced within about 10% [s10,s144]). **Backlog**: the US$103.7bn RPO converts 41%, 39% and 20% over months 1–24, 25–48 and later [s2]; with the early-Q3 commitments [s8] it covers 99% of FY2026E and 96% of FY2027E revenue but only 68% of FY2028E and 34% of FY2030E. After 2027 the model rests on capacity not yet sold: the base needs about US$33bn of new contract value in 2027 and US$59bn in 2028, against about US$80bn signed in the year to June 2026 [s2,s1]. Cost of revenue (US$3.15–3.3m per active MW-year, mostly rent and power) and capex (US$34–36m per MW energised) follow the same megawatts [s1,s2,s142]. FY2026E is the reported first half [s2] plus the model’s second half: revenue US$12.8bn (Q3 US$3.52bn, an exit-2026 run-rate of US$18.6bn), capex US$37.4bn, adjusted operating income US$1.10bn and Q3 interest of about US$890m, all inside guidance [s9]. FY2027E revenue of US$25.1bn and adjusted EBITDA of US$15.8bn sit about 5% below consensus (US$26.3bn and US$16.6bn [s64,s65]): the path adds 1.23 GW through 2027 at an even pace, where consensus implies a faster first half. FY2028E revenue of US$37.7bn is below the US$42.9bn consensus [s65] because the base builds only the 4.2 GW already contracted; the Calibration tab shows that miss. The base, with no business event on, gives **about US$105 a share**, valuing the run-rate EBITDA of the fleet in place at end-2027 against the debt that paid for it; on Section 8’s convention (FY2028 EBITDA, including the MW built during 2028) it gives about US$124 (Section 8: ≈US$119). Pick a scenario, switch events on, move a slider or choose a SOFR path, and the FY2026E–FY2030E P&L, cash bridge, funding need, interest mix, covenant tests and value per share recalculate in the browser; **Copy link** keeps the exact settings.

**Risks and upsides instead of a revenue slider.** The 24 business events in the model each carry a mechanism, a dated base rate, a probability you can edit and what to watch: data-centre delivery slips, a Vera Rubin slip, a GPU price reset or a lasting shortage, an AI capex air pocket, OpenAI re-scoping (directly and through Microsoft), Microsoft renewing less, a second-tier lab defaulting, customers turning competitor, the funding window, capital markets closing, investment-grade funding, new mega-contracts, durable inference demand, software attach, cost inflation and, as a strategic choice, buying a landlord with shares. Events in one group (delivery, GPU market, cost of capital, new contracts) exclude each other. On their own, the largest for value are a severe delivery slip (−US$61 a share), the AI capex air pocket (−US$46), capital markets closing for 2027 (−US$33: what cannot be borrowed defers about 0.5 GW by a year) and a severe GPU price reset (−US$33); the largest upsides are investment-grade funding (+US$16), a lasting GPU shortage (+US$15), software attach (+US$10) and durable inference demand (+US$9). **One probability system.** The outcome distribution takes 2,000 seeded draws of a regime (boom 25%, normal 50%, bust 25%), the 24 events (each at its catalogue probability on average, likelier in the regime it belongs to) and six uncertain drivers (exit multiple, cost of equity, capex and cost per MW, sell-through and GPU economic life): value per share has a mean of about **US$76**, a P10 of about US$17, a median of about US$70 and a P90 of about US$142, with about 38% of outcomes below the US$61.39 price (about US$113 on average in a boom, US$77 in a normal regime and US$36 in a bust). FY2028E net income runs from −US$13.8bn (P10) to −US$6.4bn (P90). **The presets are points in it, named by their causes.** The bear, “leveraged GPU leasing at the top of the cycle”, combines a mild delivery slip, a mild GPU price reset, a shut funding window, Microsoft renewing less, a second-tier lab default and customers turning competitor with 85% sell-through, a 5.5-year economic life and 6x: about US$15 a share, the 8th percentile, with interest at 46% of EBITDA in FY2027E and 51% in FY2028E. The bull, “a young AWS”, combines a lasting shortage, investment-grade funding, a new mega-contract, software attach and faster billing at 8.5x: about US$239. Restructuring stacks a severe delay, the air pocket, closed markets, the customer cuts and a four-year economic life: about US$0. Weighted by the share of outcomes nearest to each (base 54%, bear 37%, restructuring 5%, bull 4%), the presets give about US$72, close to the distribution mean and to Section 8’s ≈US$69. **Accounting life vs economic life.** The Burry-case preset depreciates GPUs over three years instead of six and gives them a three-year economic life with renewals 30% lower [s85]: FY2028E net income goes from −US$6.7bn to −US$27.4bn and adjusted operating income from US$4.2bn to −US$16.6bn, while EBITDA and cash do not move; value falls from about US$105 to about US$77, through the economic life, which sets how long the fleet earns, not through the accounting charge. **Per MW** (the unit-economics panel): a MW added in 2028 earns about US$7.3m of adjusted EBITDA a year on about US$36.9m of capex, so its five-year contract returns about 94% of the capex before interest, and with a year of renewal to a six-year life the project return is about 1%. The value therefore rests on renewals, the exit multiple and continued growth. In short, the case is not a bet on AI being real but on renting scarce machines staying valuable long enough to repay the borrowing [s213]: in the base, interest falls from 40% of EBITDA in FY2026E to 30% by FY2030E, but net income stays negative through FY2030E (−US$10.4bn) and net debt is still rising at the end of the horizon (US$113bn).

**What moves FY2027E net income** (base −US$4.7bn, or −US$7.83 a share against consensus of −US$4.49 [s64]): GPU depreciation life (3 to 7 years: −US$17.8bn to −US$2.8bn, with no change in cash), when new capex starts depreciating (on going live to six months later: −US$4.7bn to −US$0.2bn), capacity beyond the plan (+1 GW to −1 GW: −US$6.1bn to −US$3.3bn), capex per MW (US$30m to US$42m: −US$3.9bn to −US$5.9bn) and cost of revenue per MW (US$2.85m to US$3.6m: −US$3.9bn to −US$5.9bn). **Value per share** swings most with the exit multiple (5x to 9x: US$47 to US$163), the cost of equity (21% to 15%: US$75 to US$148), delivery delay (nine months late to two months early: US$40 to US$110), the economic life of GPUs (4 to 8 years: US$81 to US$144), capacity beyond the plan (±1 GW: US$74 to US$122) and the cost of new debt (14% to 9%: US$75 to US$121). **What the price implies** (Breakevens tab): at US$61.39 the shares are worth what the model says only at about 5.5x the run-rate EBITDA (we assume 7x), at prices on new deals about 44% below the path, or with new financing at about 16%. **Owned vs leased.** CoreWeave rents its data centres and owns what is inside, the fast-depreciating part [s213]: rent is about US$1.9m per leased MW-year inside cost of revenue. At 30 June it had US$35.5bn of signed leases not yet commenced (US$40.7bn at 31 March, as some commenced in Q2) on top of US$16.3bn of commenced lease liabilities [s2,s3]; the model maps them to about 4.2 GW of leased power [s10]. Those leases charge rent whether or not the GPUs arrive: when a build is deferred for lack of funding, the shell stays leased and idle, less a quarter recovered by subletting (our estimate). The self-build slider swaps rent for about US$11.5m per MW of shell and power capex over 25 years [s147], only for MW beyond the signed leases; the base assumes 10% of those from 2027 (220 MW owned by 2030, including the 40 MW at Kenilworth [s154]). **The NVIDIA backstop** pays for half of the capacity a stress leaves unsold, up to US$6.3bn through April 2032 [s20]: in the bear it buys US$5.5bn by 2030, and in the restructuring the whole US$6.3bn. It is a floor, and a circular one, since NVIDIA is also the supplier and a shareholder [s62].

blocks.title: Fixed vs floating: how much of the interest moves with SOFR
blocks.text: **Today.** Of about US$42.2bn of principal after the August and September financings (US$35.6bn at 30 June [s2], plus the US$1.2bn DDTL 5.5 and US$1.2bn revolver draws [s2,s216] and the US$4.2bn 2.875% convertible [s14]), about US$14.6bn (35%) is priced over SOFR by contract: DDTL 1.0, 2.0, 2.1, 3.0, 5.0 and 5.5, the DDTL 4.0 floating tranche and the revolver [s127,s128,s129,s103,s17,s104,s59]. CoreWeave swaps part of it: interest-rate swaps rose to US$4,661m of notional at 30 June from US$319m at end-2025 [s2,s1]. DDTL 3.0 must swap at least 75% and DDTL 5.0 at least 95% [s1,s2]; we attribute about US$2.8bn of the swaps to their drawn balances, at about 3.45% and 3.85% (our estimates; the rates are not disclosed [s210]). After swaps about **US$11.8bn (28%) floats** and US$30.3bn (72%) is fixed: senior notes at 8.5–9.75% (the euro notes swapped to dollars at about 9.7%, our estimate [s2,s211]), convertibles at 1.75–2.875%, OEM financing at about 9–11% and the fixed DDTL 4.0 tranche [s2]. At October SOFR that puts about 34% of the interest bill on floating rates; in Q2 2026 about 43% of contractual interest was on floating loans and about 38% reset with SOFR after swaps (our arithmetic from [s2]); the 10-Q’s own +100bp figure (about US$122m a year) ignores the swaps [s2]. **Ahead.** The floating share falls as the DDTLs amortise and as DDTL 4.0 hedges at least 95% of its floating draws after June 2027 [s2]: unhedged floating debt is about US$14.9bn at end-2026 (after the committed draws), US$7.6bn at end-2027 and US$5.2bn at end-2028. New borrowing is the rest. Half is assumed raised floating, DDTL-style, and 60% of that swapped when raised, so about 20% of new debt resets with SOFR; fixed new debt locks its year’s rate. **Floating share of interest**: 35% in H2 2026E, then 27%, 20%, 18% and 15%. **+100bp on SOFR** from November 2026 adds about US$348m to FY2027E interest, US$692m to FY2028E, US$972m to FY2029E and US$1,197m to FY2030E (+200bp: US$701m, US$1,399m, US$1,977m and US$2,454m; exact re-runs of the model). Only about US$160–210m a year of the +100bp is floating debt resetting; the rest is new fixed debt issued at the higher rate. So the new-debt mix changes when the rate risk lands, not how big it is: raising 85% floating with 25% swapped lifts the floating share of FY2028E interest to 50%, against 8% at 30% floating and 95% swapped, but the FY2028E +100bp cost barely moves (US$703m against US$687m). **What fixing protects.** The same +150bp shock starting in January 2028 instead of now (the late-shock preset) adds nothing to FY2027E interest and US$468m to FY2028E, against US$524m and US$1,044m if it starts now, because by then DDTL 4.0’s floating draws are swapped and the 2026–27 borrowing is mostly fixed. Value barely differs (about US$91 either way): it moves through the exit multiple’s cost-of-capital re-rating, which sees the 2028 rate whenever the shock starts. +100bp takes about US$10 off value per share (US$105 to US$95) and +200bp about US$18; an exit at end-2030, which sees the interest bill to 2030, gives the same answer within a dollar. **Paths.** SOFR follows market forwards as of 15 October 2026: 3.85% for H2 2026, then 4.45%, 4.65%, 4.60% and 4.45% (2030 is our assumption) [s122,s111]. The Fed’s September projections run 0, 35, 65, 85 and 100bp below that [s119,s120,s121] and give about US$111 a share; our faster-cuts path about US$119 and our re-hike path about US$99. **Funding.** Gaps are met first from about US$10.2bn of committed facilities (DDTL 3.0, 4.0, 5.0 and 5.5 and the revolver [s2,s17,s104,s59,s216]), then by new debt at about 10.5% [s59,s28,s31], the floating part amortising over five years from contract cash. Gross new borrowing is about US$36bn in FY2027E, US$32bn in FY2028E and US$23bn in FY2029E: the build needs open capital markets every year [s213]. When a gap cannot be borrowed, the model defers the MW it would have paid for by a year (and their revenue) rather than running cash below zero; whatever is still short pays a penalty rate. The unsecured notes reportedly cap total leverage at 6.0x and secured leverage at 4.0x [s137]; tested on the last quarter’s EBITDA × 4, base total leverage is 4.5x at end-2026, then 4.2x and 3.7x (on full-year EBITDA it would read 6.9x in FY2026E, which overstates a company whose EBITDA doubles in a year), and about 3% of the distribution’s outcomes cross a cap from FY2027E.

blocks.title: What the model leaves out
blocks.text: FY2026 is held at guidance in every preset: the capacity sliders and events start in January 2027 (funding events from November 2026). The events are linked only through the regime (boom, normal, bust) and the exclusive groups; the regime probabilities and lifts are our judgement, so the distribution’s tails are as good as that judgement. A delay shifts the MW and most of their GPU capex; the contracted revenue of the late months moves past the end of the contract, outside the horizon, because delayed contracts extend rather than lapse [s145], and no delivery credits are modelled. When funding is short the model defers builds by a year (the signed leases keep charging rent), then charges a penalty rate on any gap left. The NVIDIA backstop is credited at half the value of the capacity a stress leaves unsold, because the order’s pricing and how much of it is already used are not disclosed [s20]. Customer shares beyond the 10-Q’s lettered customers, the swap rates, the sublet recovery and the share of new debt raised floating are our estimates. There are no tax-loss carry-forwards (a tax charge of about US$290m a year stands in for the tax CoreWeave books in loss years), no interest on cash, no capitalised interest and no default mechanics: below zero the equity value floors at nothing, and a covenant breach is flagged rather than stopping the borrowing. Convertibles are debt at face, with net shares only above their capped-call caps. It is a tool for testing assumptions, not a forecast.

blocks.title: Short answer: nothing flagged it
blocks.text: No GIVA module named CoreWeave, flagged its share-price slide, or warned about the balance-sheet and credit risk behind it before the week of 12–16 October. CoreWeave has never appeared on the published dashboard [s99]. The miss is structural: several independent gaps each blocked it, and fixing any single one would not have produced the call.

The only related signal was generic and at market level. In every weekly run between 1 August and 12 October (nine runs; none was recorded for 17, 24 or 31 August), our market models flagged the Nasdaq, S&P 500, technology, semiconductor and software indices and the growth-style (IVW) and momentum-factor (MTUM) index proxies as **overvalued**, with value scores between about 2 and 19 out of 100 (below 3 for the Nasdaq and semiconductors), according to our internal prediction logs. Nothing connected that to AI infrastructure or to debt-funded capex, and our Analyst agent never selected those markets for review.

blocks.caption: Module-by-module audit (as of the 12 October dashboard refresh; internal records)
rows: Scored CRWV, but with no market cap or multiples

No share count in our store: CRWV has three share classes and the EDGAR feed we use drops per-class cover-page facts. CRWV and 218 other priced securities share the gap, and no quality check flagged it

A missing valuation input is treated as average for its peer group. In a replication of our 2 October scoring run, CRWV ranked around the 87th percentile of technology peers on value, and across the universe roughly 300 of about 330 stocks with no valuation inputs scored "Cheap"
By design they need P/E above zero, three years of annual history and a US$2bn market cap; a loss-making 2025 IPO can never qualify
Debt and capex are ingested but not scored; there is no leverage, interest-cover, cash-burn or credit input

The stock-screener snapshot had not been created yet; once live, CRWV would be hidden by default (short-history data flag). No drawdown, 1-month or 200-day fields exist, so a user could not build a "fell more than 20%" alert
The events table is empty; we ingest no news, 8-K items or credit events
Its candidate pools exclude overvalued or frothy markets; its 12 October run produced no theses (all eight attempts failed to parse)
Tagged as prepackaged software (SIC 7372) and ranked against all technology stocks
Neither is the right peer group for a GPU-infrastructure company

blocks.text: **Would better data have helped?** Only partly. With the public share count injected, CRWV would no longer have read as "Cheap" on value against technology peers; it would score very high on fundamental growth and still fail our compounder rules. It would not have warned, because the risk that actually moved the stock (refinancing and credit) is not modelled.
